You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Below are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

=== TRANSCRIPTS ===
# Interview — a fleet technician

Interviewer: Hello! To get started, could you tell me which company you work for and walk me through an ordinary working day from start to finish?

Interviewee: I work at one of the drone operating companies. During an ordinary working day, I keep drones and charging equipment in working order, add new drones to our fleet, and retire old ones. I also set up charging pads at our sites, take drones out of service for repairs and put them back, and send drones to charge.

Interviewer: Could you walk me through what happens first thing when you start your shift, and how you decide what to work on first?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How do you find out that a drone needs repair or charging, or who hands that work over to you?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you finish repairing a drone or putting a new one into the fleet, who do you hand it over to, or who needs to know it's ready?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Could you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When something goes wrong with a drone or a charging pad, what do you need to know right away?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What do you currently check by hand because you don't trust how it's reported or tracked today?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are you most afraid a new software service would get wrong in your work?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you add a new drone to the fleet or set up a charging pad at a site, what information do you need to record about it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you take a drone out of service for repairs or retire an old one, what steps do you take?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How do you decide which charging pad to send a drone to when it needs to charge?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: คิด
The interviewee is answering "I don't know" to everything after the first question. Every required topic has been asked about, and follow-ups no longer bring anything new. I should end the interview.END OF INTERVIEW

Interviewee: Thank you for the questions, but I have to get back to keeping our drones and charging equipment in working order. Let's wrap up here.

---

# Interview — a dispatcher

Interviewer: Could you walk me through a typical shift for you, from the moment you sit down at your desk to when you hand over and leave?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: To start small, which of the drone operating companies do you work for, and what is the very first thing you do when you log in each day?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Thinking about the last drone flight you dealt with, what was your involvement in it?

Interviewee: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, meaning I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can also call off a flight. However, I know nothing about software and accounts and passwords inside the service are not used since staff accounts are issued by the platform company outside it.

Interviewer: How does a request for a flight first reach you, and who does it come from?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When you are deciding which drone flies along which way, what information do you look at to make that decision?

Interviewee: I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts, but our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us. I can also call off a flight.

Interviewer: How do you work out today which of your drones could get to where a job starts?

Interviewee: I want help finding out which of my drones could get to where a job starts. However, our policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us, and choosing the drone and the way it flies is my legal responsibility.

Interviewer: What details about a drone or a job do you need to see to tell if that drone can reach where the job starts?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Before you sign off a flight to leave, what do you check by hand because you don't trust anyone or anything else to get it right?

Interviewee: I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. I can call off a flight, and it is my legal responsibility to choose the drone and the way it flies.

Interviewer: What makes you decide to call off a flight?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Thinking back over the last few months, what was your worst day on the job, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I worry about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and about closures coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on, and batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

Interviewer: When a drone restarts in flight or radio coverage drops out, what happens on your end, and what do you need to know right after it comes back?

Interviewee: I worry about radio coverage being patchy, especially around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and about reports from drones arriving late, out of order, more than once, or not at all through relay stations. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.

Interviewer: When a closure comes into force while drones are already in the air, how do you find out about it, and what do you have to do right away?

Interviewee: I worry that a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.

Interviewer: When a sudden closure applies at once or an area is widened, how do you check if any of your drones are affected?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned reports from drones arriving late, out of order, or more than once through relay stations—what problems does that cause for you when you are watching a flight?

Interviewee: I worry because nobody watches every drone at every moment, and one person may be responsible for hundreds. Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, causing reports from drones to arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.

Interviewer: Since one person may be responsible for hundreds of drones and cannot watch every one at every moment, how do you know when something has gone wrong with one of them?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a drone has an issue—like a battery draining faster than planned or an incident on a flight—what do you need to find out or look back at right afterward?

Interviewee: I worry that batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. I do not know what I need to find out or look back at right afterward.

Interviewer: How do you work with the fleet technicians and the airspace desk—what do they hand over to you, and what do you hand over to them?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What are you most afraid a new service would get wrong or do badly for your work?

Interviewee: I worry about closures coming into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, and about radio coverage being patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather. I also worry that reports from drones can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all.

Interviewer: Thinking about your company's fleet, jobs, and sites compared to the other operating companies on the platform, what are your concerns or rules around who can see what?

Interviewee: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. We accept sharing airspace information because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

Interviewer: Are there any other parts of your job, rules you must follow, or problems you deal with that we haven't talked about yet?

Interviewee: I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies along which way before signing off a flight. I also follow the EU drone operation rules and the EU U-space rules. Furthermore, personal data of staff is covered by the GDPR.

Interviewer: Under the EU drone operation and U-space rules, what records or proof of your sign-offs and decisions do you need to keep?

Interviewee: I don't know.

---

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

Interviewer: Could you walk me through an ordinary working day for you, from the moment you start your shift until you finish?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: That's okay. Let's start smaller: what is the very first thing you do when you sit down at the airspace desk in the morning?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Thinking back to your most recent shift, what was one task you worked on?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which involves the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. When a closure is entered, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers.

Interviewer: When the authorities announce a closure, how does that information reach you, and what do you do with it step by step?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned wanting to know how much disruption a closure caused across customers—what specific things do you look at to measure that disruption?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Can you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Right after a sudden airspace closure or something going wrong, what do you need to know immediately?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything in your current work that you check by hand because you don't fully trust the existing tools or data?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When we build this new service for the airspace desk, what are you most afraid it might get wrong?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: During your work, who hands information or tasks to you, and who do you hand your work off to?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: You mentioned earlier that you deal with flight corridors between sites and the zones that group them—what exactly do you do to set up or change those corridors and zones?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a closure happens, what makes a flight count as disrupted for one of the customer companies?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What information can you see about the customer companies, given that their operations are private from each other?

Interviewee: Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business, and I have no business looking into any one company's operations. The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do, but they accept sharing airspace information because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

Interviewer: Since you can't look into any one company's operations, yet you want to know how much disruption a closure caused across customers, what kind of summary or numbers are you allowed to see?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a closure is announced by the authorities, does it apply to specific flight corridors, or to entire zones?

Interviewee: The authorities define zones where flying is prohibited, and they announce planned closures with a start and end time or sudden ones that apply at once. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.

Interviewer: When a closure is amended—like an area widening or an end time moving—what happens on your end?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: How do the zones defined by the authorities connect to the flight corridors between sites?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which consists of the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. Sites also have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time.

Interviewer: Since each company's sites are its own business, how do sites fit into the shared network of flight corridors that you keep?

Interviewee: I keep the shared picture of the airspace, which includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones that group them, and the closures announced by the authorities. Sites have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business.

Interviewer: How do you interact with the dispatchers or fleet technicians at the customer companies, if at all?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: What happens when a sudden closure is announced that applies at once? How do the customer companies find out about it?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: When a new customer company joins the platform, what needs to be added to the shared airspace picture?

Interviewee: I don't know.

Interviewer: Is there anything else about the airspace desk, the flight corridors, the zones, or the closures that you think is important for me to know?

Interviewee: A closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. The authorities announce planned closures with a start and end time, as well as sudden ones that apply at once, and they are often amended during the day.

Interviewer: When a closure comes into force while drones of several companies are already in the air, what needs to happen with those drones or the airspace desk?

Interviewee: I don't know.
=== END OF TRANSCRIPTS ===

Write the requirements for the service: what it must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does. Rest every requirement on what the interviews say.

Write them as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, and nothing else:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
